title: TypeScript 6 vs 7 on type-fest
question: How much faster does TypeScript 7 type-check a real, type-heavy library than TypeScript 6, and how much of the gain comes from the native compiler itself rather than parallel checking? What happens to memory on a heavy workload?
verdict: On an Apple M3 Pro ({{m3.cores}} cores), TypeScript 7.0.2 checked the type-fest sources {{m3.total}} faster than TypeScript 6.0.3 ({{m3.ts7}} vs {{m3.ts6}}): {{m3.native}} comes from the native compiler alone (single-threaded) and {{m3.parallel}} from parallel checking. On the full suite with type tests, TypeScript 6 stops at Node.js's default heap limit ({{heap.default}}); with a {{heap.large}} heap it finishes in {{full.ts6}}, against {{full.ts7}} for TypeScript 7 ({{full.total}} faster), but TypeScript 7 peaks higher in memory ({{full.rss.ts7}} RSS vs {{full.rss.ts6}}). Stays open until a second machine is measured with the same protocol.
takeaway: Most of the gain comes from the native compiler, so expect it even on small CI runners. The default mode does not use all available cores: on this {{m3.cores}}-core machine, `--checkers 8` checked the sources in {{chk.c8}}, {{chk.c8.gain}} faster than the default mode ({{m3.ts7}}), and `--checkers 4` took {{chk.c4}}.
notes: Types and Instantiations differ between TypeScript 6 and 7 on identical code, so never compare these counters across compilers. TypeScript 7's counters also vary slightly from run to run on the full suite, single-threaded included; on the library sources they are identical across runs.

Memory is peak resident memory (RSS) from `/usr/bin/time -l`, field "maximum resident set size", of the largest process: the Node.js process for TypeScript 6, the native compiler for TypeScript 7 (its launcher replaces itself with the native binary). It is not the compiler's own "Memory used" line, which for TypeScript 6 is the V8 heap.

Out of memory means Node.js's default heap limit ({{heap.default}} here), not the machine's RAM: TypeScript 6 aborted with "Reached heap limit" at {{full.ts6.oom.rss}} RSS, and completed with `--max-old-space-size=16384`.
One library (type-fest at one commit), check time only: no emit, watch mode or editor latency.

The two machines differ by CPU as well as core count, so compare conditions within a machine; the comparison between machines is indicative only. On the {{xeon.cores}}-core Intel Xeon, parallel checking gives {{xeon.parallel}} ({{xeon.parallel.range}}) and the native compiler {{xeon.native}}.

The Intel Xeon results use the earlier protocol: {{xeon.runs}} runs, no warm-up, not interleaved, no RSS. The Apple M3 Pro results use a discarded warm-up per condition and interleaved runs, with other applications open (load average {{load.min}} to {{load.max}}). The full-suite runs stay noisy: up to {{full.cv.max}} coefficient of variation.

The checker series was measured with other applications open (load average {{chk.load.min}} to {{chk.load.max}}), and in a separate series from the default mode: the comparison between `--checkers 8` and the default mode crosses two series.
